minimum_safe_summary: This doctoral thesis investigates the impact of noise, particularly background speech intelligibility (measured by STI and distraction distance), on cognitive performance and subjective reactions in open-plan offices, and explores design solutions. Comprising three laboratory experiments and two field studies, the research found that intelligible background speech impairs verbal short-term and working memory and increases subjective disturbance. More complex tasks were generally unaffected. Office distractions, including noise, mediated negative changes in environmental satisfaction, collaboration, and stress symptoms following office relocations. Masking sounds (filtered pink noise, spring water) improved acoustic satisfaction and performance, while music was less effective. Holistic room acoustic design and the provision of easily accessible quiet workspaces were identified as effective solutions, though benefits of acoustic design were limited at short distances. Limitations include the generalizability of lab tasks, student participants, and the retrospective design of field studies.
